transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Rodriguez (BrightScale Head of ML), Tom Nguyen (BrightScale Infra), Lena Park (BrightScale Security)

Summary: SE demo and tuning session; lots of config knobs; agreed next steps around pilot and docs.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Avery): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll run about an hour, Samir will lead the technical part, I'll handle next steps. Maya, you good?
00:12 Speaker 2 (Maya): Yeah, thanks. We have Tom and Lena here, we're trying to get throughput up for our chat product, p99 under 350ms is ideal but cost is a concern.
00:25 Speaker 3 (Samir): Great. Quick agenda: continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, token limits), KV cache tuning, quantization impact, and then VPC/private deployment notes. We'll look at numbers and config.
00:40 Speaker 2 (Maya): Sounds good. Our current stack: mixed GPU cluster on-prem, some nodes on GCP. We're testing Redwood Dedicated for predictable capacity. Typical requests are 32-64 tokens in prompt, response ~60-120 tokens. Burstiness at EOD.
01:05 Speaker 3 (Samir): Okay cool. First, continuous batching — Redwood's runtime keeps a short scheduling window and builds batches from inflight requests to maximize GPU utilization while respecting latency SLOs. The key knobs are scheduling_window_ms and max_num_seqs.
01:30 Speaker 1 (Avery): Quick clarification — max_num_seqs controls how many concurrent sequences we allow into a single decoding batch, right?
01:36 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yeah, essentially. If you set max_num_seqs=8, the scheduler will try to pack up to eight sequences per step, so you get better throughput but p99 can climb. For chat workloads with short outputs, higher max_num_seqs usually wins on tokens/sec.
01:58 Speaker 4 (Tom): Do we have recommended starting points for our load profile? We're seeing lots of 1-2 request bursts from mobile clients.
02:10 Speaker 3 (Samir): For mobile-y taily loads, start with max_num_seqs=4 and scheduling_window_ms=25, then bump to 8 if p99 stays within target. Also consider enabling prefix/KV cache to fold repeated context and reduce effective sequence length.
02:35 Speaker 2 (Maya): KV cache — our prompts reuse user history a lot. How does cache hit rate affect batching?
02:44 Speaker 3 (Samir): If cache hits are high, effective token generation is lower, so batches fill faster because the runtime doesn't re-execute earlier tokens; that helps throughput. But watch for excessive cache evictions on large conversational histories. We usually recommend trimming or summarizing long history beyond N tokens to keep KV working.
03:10 Speaker 4 (Tom): Any concrete numbers you can share? Like tokens/sec with max_num_seqs 4 vs 8 for a 70-token output on A100-like hardware?
03:18 Speaker 3 (Samir): Rough numbers, ballpark: on an A100 equivalent, single-seq throughput might be ~30-40 tokens/s. With max_num_seqs=4 you can hit ~120-150 tokens/s, with 8 around 200-250 tokens/s, depending on attention optimizations and quantization. p99 latencies change — single-seq p99 might be 250-300ms, with 8 it can go to 450-600ms if scheduling window is long.
03:50 Speaker 2 (Maya): That matches what we feared. Our p99 target is 350ms. So we probably need to trade off to keep under target.
04:05 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yep; that's the latency vs cost tradeoff. There are also scheduler policies: latency-first, throughput-first, and cost-aware modes. For BrightScale I'd suggest latency-first with adaptive batching, which keeps scheduling windows small but uses max_num_seqs opportunistically.
04:28 Speaker 4 (Tom): What's adaptive batching?
04:33 Speaker 3 (Samir): The runtime adapts the scheduling window based on observed qps and queue depth. If traffic is high, it relaxes window to form bigger batches; if traffic drops, it tightens to meet latency SLOs. You can fix it to a policy or let it run auto.
04:50 Speaker 2 (Maya): Can we pin to a deterministic behavior for compliance? We prefer predictable latencies.
04:57 Speaker 3 (Samir): You can pin scheduling_window_ms and max_num_seqs explicitly, or opt into adaptive with explicit bounds (min/max window, max_num_seqs cap). That gives predictability while still getting benefits under load.
05:20 Speaker 1 (Avery): Quick note on token limits — you mentioned per-request token cap?
05:24 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yes, runtime enforces token_limit_per_request and token_limit_per_seq. Long requests can blow up compute. For chat we enforce a prompt+output cap; trimming strategies help. Also there's a per-batch token budget to avoid OOMs during decoding.
05:44 Speaker 4 (Tom): How does quantization factor into throughput/latency? We plan to use int8 for latency but worried about quality regressions.
05:55 Speaker 3 (Samir): Quantization reduces compute and memory bandwidth; int8 usually gives ~1.5x-2x throughput improvement, int4 can be bigger but more quality risk. For chat LLMs we often recommend per-layer mixed quant (some layers float16) or using Redwood's verified quant profiles — we can share the spreadsheet with eval deltas.
06:22 Speaker 2 (Maya): Would quantization change scheduler behavior?
06:26 Speaker 3 (Samir): Indirectly — faster kernels reduce per-token time, which lowers queueing pressure; scheduler will adjust batches to keep GPUs fed. In practice you might be able to increase max_num_seqs without hitting latency SLO.
06:42 Speaker 4 (Tom): About KV cache memory — with many user sessions we may run out of RAM on the serving pods. Any guidance?
06:51 Speaker 3 (Samir): We have evictions policies: LRU per-user, session-size caps, and optional tiering to disk for cold cache. For on-prem you might increase host memory or shard KV across pods. Also consider compressing history or using summarized state to keep KV small.
07:15 Speaker 2 (Maya): Security question — if we do VPC/private deployment, does KV stay inside customer network? Lena, want to chime in on requirements.
07:27 Speaker 5 (Lena): Yes we need all KV and logs to be customer-controlled, encrypted with our KMS. SOC2 is required, also audit logs for access to user histories.
07:38 Speaker 3 (Samir): In Private mode the KV store and control plane are customer-managed; we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. We'll share the private deployment architecture.
07:50 Speaker 1 (Avery): Back to tuning — let's walk through a sample config for your expected traffic. Samir, can you pull up the recommended baseline?
07:58 Speaker 3 (Samir): Sure. Baseline for BrightScale chat: scheduling_window_ms=25, max_num_seqs=4, token_limit_per_request=1024, per_batch_token_budget=4096, kv_eviction_policy=LRU, quant_profile="int8-mixed-verified". If p99 under 350ms, bump max_num_seqs->6 then 8 and monitor.
08:26 Speaker 4 (Tom): What about worker size — number of concurrent model workers per GPU? We run pods with 1 model replica per GPU but consider multi-model packing.
08:38 Speaker 3 (Samir): We recommend one replica per GPU for low-latency chatting. For throughput-oriented background workloads, model packing and multiple replicas can be used. Also kernel selection matters — when sequence lengths are short, certain kernels are faster. We'll share kernel profile mappings.
09:00 Speaker 2 (Maya): Could we see a quick benchmark you ran earlier? You mentioned numbers.
09:05 Speaker 3 (Samir): I have a quick paste: test on A100-40GB equivalent, model X (redwood-ggml style), prompt 40 tokens, response 80 tokens: max_num_seqs=1 -> 35 tok/s, p99=280ms; max_num_seqs=4 -> 140 tok/s, p99=320ms; max_num_seqs=8 -> 220 tok/s, p99=540ms. With int8 quant -> +1.7x tokens/s and p99 drops ~10-15% in practice.
09:40 Speaker 4 (Tom): Does that p99 include scheduling delay?
09:44 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yes includes scheduler and decode. The scheduling window contributed ~60-90ms at high batching levels in that run.
10:00 Speaker 2 (Maya): Okay. For our SLO we might aim for max_num_seqs=6 with quant int8 and a shorter scheduling_window_ms, maybe 20ms.
10:12 Speaker 3 (Samir): That seems reasonable. We'll want to run a pilot with traffic replay to validate.
10:20 Speaker 1 (Avery): On the pilot, Tom will provide traffic traces and token distribution. Samir will produce config and benchmark scripts. We'll run on Dedicated to match SLAs.
10:32 Speaker 4 (Tom): Regarding Dedicated vs Hosted — we need data residency and tight network controls so Dedicated or Private is required. Any differences in tuning between Dedicated and Private on-prem?
10:45 Speaker 3 (Samir): Tuning knobs are the same. Differences are in hardware variability and network egress latencies. On-prem sometimes has noisier neighbors; set conservative per-batch budgets and monitor GPU saturation. Also be wary of NUMA and PCIe topology for KV memory locality.
11:10 Speaker 5 (Lena): For Private deployment we need to run a security review. Can you send the deployment checklist?
11:17 Speaker 1 (Avery): Yes, we'll include SOC2 report, network diagrams, KMS integration guide.
11:24 Speaker 2 (Maya): A couple more questions: 1) how does the runtime handle partial batches (low qps), 2) can we pre-warm KV for expected active users?
11:35 Speaker 3 (Samir): 1) Partial batches are dispatched after scheduling_window_ms or when max_num_seqs hit; if qps is low we see smaller batches and lower throughput. 2) You can pre-warm KV by seeding session history into cache during off-peak or on login; that improves first request latencies. There is a prewarm API we can document.
12:02 Speaker 4 (Tom): Any gotchas on quantization for on-prem? For example, driver versions or kernel compatibility?
12:10 Speaker 3 (Samir): Yes, some old drivers break int8 kernels; we maintain a compatibility matrix. Also performance varies with CUDA/cuDNN versions. We'll share the matrix in the doc pack.
12:28 Speaker 2 (Maya): Can we run A/B between int8 and float16 for quality checks quickly?
12:33 Speaker 3 (Samir): Absolutely — we can run parallel endpoints and route a percentage of traffic. Redwood supports canary/AB rollouts with automatic fallback to float16 if quality regressions detected by your eval prompts.
12:50 Speaker 4 (Tom): About monitoring — what metrics should we watch?
12:55 Speaker 3 (Samir): Key metrics: GPU utilization, tokens/sec, per-request latency p50/p95/p99, scheduler queue depth, KV cache hit rate, eviction rate, memory pressure, and error/retry counts. We'll provide dashboards that map these to suggested actions.
13:20 Speaker 1 (Avery): Great. Let's recap next steps.
13:25 Speaker 2 (Maya): Recap please.
13:27 Speaker 1 (Avery): 1) Samir to send baseline config and scheduler knobs doc. 2) Avery to send quantization recommendations & verified profiles. 3) Tom to share traffic traces and token distributions. 4) Schedule pilot starting 2026-06-15 on Dedicated. 5) Lena to receive security + SOC2 docs.
13:45 Speaker 2 (Maya): That matches our expectations. Thanks, folks.
13:50 Speaker 3 (Samir): Thanks — we'll follow up in email with artifacts and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
13:58 Speaker 1 (Avery): End of meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard words (e.g., model name transcription), filler and overlap present.
